title: Five fixes for your Google Business Profile this week
dek: For a restaurant, shop or repair business, the Google Business Profile is often the first thing people see. Five small fixes make it complete, current and easy to trust.

body.p: When someone searches for a business like yours, the profile on Google Search and Maps usually shows up before your website does. It answers the first questions people have: are you open, where are you, what do others say. Here are five fixes you can make in an afternoon.

body.h: 1. Choose the most specific primary category

body.p: The primary category tells Google what you are. Pick the most specific one that fits, such as "Turkish restaurant" rather than "Restaurant", then add secondary categories for anything else you offer.
Wrong hours cost visits and invite bad reviews. Update regular hours, set special hours for holidays ahead of time, and check them again after any change in staffing or season.

body.h: 3. Add real photos, and keep adding them

body.p: Show the storefront as people see it from the street, the inside, the team and your best products or dishes. Replace photos that no longer match what customers will find when they arrive.

Thank people for good reviews by name and mention something specific. For critical ones, stay calm, keep it short and offer to continue the conversation directly. Future customers read the replies as much as the reviews.

body.h: 5. Fill in services and post updates

body.p: List your main products or services with a one-line description each. Use posts for offers, events and news so the profile looks looked-after rather than abandoned.
None of these takes more than an hour. Done together, they turn a bare listing into a profile that answers questions before people have to ask.

title: Why a posting calendar beats posting more
dek: People rarely remember how often you posted. They remember whether your feed felt consistent and worth following. A simple calendar gets you there with less effort.

body.p: Many businesses treat social media as a daily scramble: something has to go up today, so whatever is at hand goes up. The result is a feed that looks busy but says very little. A calendar fixes that, and it usually means less work, not more.

Choose three or four recurring themes that matter to your customers. For a restaurant that might be signature dishes, the people in the kitchen, events and guest moments. Every post belongs to one theme, so the feed tells a clear story over time.

body.h: Plan a month, produce in batches

body.p: Map the month on one page: which theme goes on which day, and which dates matter, such as holidays, launches and local events. Then shoot and write in batches. One focused session can cover weeks of content.

ul: Early week: a product, dish or service, shown well.
Midweek: behind the scenes, the people and the process.
End of week: customers, community or an offer for the weekend.

body.p: A calendar is a plan, not a cage. Keep a slot free each week for something timely, like a busy night, a new arrival or a local event, so the feed still feels alive.
Look at which posts were saved, shared or brought in messages, not only likes. Do more of what worked and drop what didn't. Over a few months the calendar gets sharper and the results follow.

title: How to prepare for a brand photo shoot
dek: Good shoots are decided before the camera comes out. A little preparation means better pictures, a shorter day and photos you will still be using a year from now.

body.p: A photo shoot is an investment, and most of its value is set in the days before it. Here is how we prepare with clients so the day runs smoothly and every picture has a job.

body.h: Start from where the photos will live

body.p: List the places the images will be used: website header, menu or catalog, social posts, Stories, ads. Each has its own shape, so the shot list should include both horizontal and vertical versions of the important pictures.

Turn that list into specific shots: the storefront, the hero product from three angles, the team at work, a detail of the materials. A shot list keeps the day focused and makes sure nothing important is forgotten.

body.h: Prepare the space and the products

ul: Clean and declutter every area that will be in frame.
Choose the best-looking items and keep spares ready.
For restaurants, shoot before service when the light and the kitchen are calm.

body.p: Decide who will appear and share simple wardrobe guidance: solid colors, no large logos, clothes that fit the brand. Collect permission from anyone who will be recognizable in the published photos.

Select the strongest frames, edit them to one consistent look and organize the archive with clear names and folders. A well-kept library means the team can find the right photo in seconds, long after the shoot day.
